statement: Among US civilian adults living in households in 2015 and 2016, past-year misuse of benzodiazepines (any use other than as a doctor directed, by self-report) was reported by 2.2% (95% CI 2.0 to 2.3), against 10.4% (10.1 to 10.7) who reported using them only as prescribed; the people reporting misuse most often gave relaxing or relieving tension (47.1%) or help with sleep (26.6%) as their main reason, and getting high less often (11.6%), and most often got the pills from a friend or relative (68.8% in all, editors' sum). Certainty: low. Status: single study. The figures come from the National Survey on Drug Use and Health (NSDUH), a national probability survey answered by computer, partly in a private audio-assisted section meant to encourage honest answers, in 86,186 adults (Maust et al., 2019). In all, 12.6% (12.2 to 12.9) reported past-year benzodiazepine use, an estimated 30.6 million adults a year, so misuse made up 17.2% of use (5.3 million people against 25.3 million). Misuse counted taking a benzodiazepine without a prescription and taking one's own in greater amounts, more often or for longer than prescribed, and anyone reporting any misuse in the past year counted as misusing even if they also took it as prescribed. It was most common at ages 18 to 25 (5.2% of all adults that age; 51.0% of their benzodiazepine use) and least common at 65 or older (0.6%). Of the 2,533 people reporting misuse, 73.9% had taken a benzodiazepine without a prescription; the one misused was most often alprazolam (Xanax; 75.1%), then diazepam (20.5%), clonazepam (20.0%) and lorazepam (15.4%), some people naming more than one. Their main reasons, from a list: to relax or relieve tension 47.1%, to help with sleep 26.6%, to get high 11.6%, to help with feelings or emotions 10.1%, to experiment 6.0%, to increase or decrease the effects of another drug 1.6%, and 'hooked or have to have it' 0.6%. These shares add to 103.6% (editors' sum; 104.0% at ages 18 to 49 and 101.3% at 50 or older), more than rounding can explain, and 'another reason', also on the list, is not shown; the paper does not say whether people could give more than one main reason, so the shares cannot be read as exactly one reason per person. Getting high was the main reason for 13.9% at ages 18 to 49 and 3.0% at 50 or older, and sleep for 22.4% and 41.7%. Sources: free from a friend or relative 53.2%, bought from one 12.3% and stolen from one 3.3%, one doctor 19.5%, two or more doctors 0.9%, bought from a dealer or stranger 7.7%, and stolen from a health care setting 0.1% (together 97.0%, editors' sum; the rest not shown). Of the people reporting misuse, 4.6% (3.7 to 5.6) met DSM-IV criteria for past-year abuse and 6.8% (5.6 to 8.2) for past-year dependence, and they reported a mean of 5.4 days of misuse in the past month (whether people with no misuse that month are counted is not stated). Among people who used benzodiazepines, misuse rather than use as prescribed went with younger age, being male, and use, misuse or use disorders of alcohol, marijuana, prescription opioids and prescription stimulants, a cross-sectional association that shows nothing about cause. All of it is self-report without checks; adults in institutions and on active military duty are not covered; response rates are not given; and the 2015 redesign of the survey means the figures cannot be compared with earlier years. The authors suggest that part of what the survey counts as misuse may be people treating anxiety or insomnia that has gone untreated because of poor access to care; the analysis did not test this.
plain: Why do people misuse benzos like Xanax? In a big US survey in 2015 and 2016, about 13 in 100 adults said they had taken a benzodiazepine in the past year, and about 2 in 100 said they had misused one, meaning any use a doctor did not direct, such as taking pills without a prescription (the most common kind) or taking more of their own than prescribed. Three in four of the people who misused one had misused alprazolam (Xanax). Asked for their main reason, 47 in 100 said to relax or relieve tension, 27 in 100 to sleep, 12 in 100 to get high and 10 in 100 to cope with feelings; these shares add up to a little over 100, and the paper does not explain why. About 69 in 100 got the pills from a friend or relative, mostly for free. About 7 in 100 of the people who misused benzos met the criteria for dependence. These are people's own answers, not checked, and the survey did not include people living in institutions, such as prisons, or on active military duty.
population: US civilian adults aged 18 or older living in households, National Survey on Drug Use and Health 2015 and 2016 (86,186 respondents; 10,290 reporting past-year benzodiazepine use; 2,533 reporting misuse, 2,357 of them aged 18 to 49 and 176 aged 50 or older); people in institutions and on active military duty not covered
exposure: Self-reported past-year benzodiazepine use, only as prescribed or with misuse (any use other than as a doctor directed: without a prescription, or in greater amounts, more often or longer than prescribed), reported in the survey's tranquilizer and sedative sections
comparator: None for the shares among people reporting misuse (descriptive); use only as prescribed, for the share of use that was misuse and for the factors that went with misuse; ages 18 to 49 against 50 or older
outcome: Self-reported past-year use and misuse; among people reporting misuse, its type, main reason (from a list), source and the benzodiazepine misused; days of misuse in the past month; DSM-IV abuse and dependence
magnitude: Maust et al. (2019), NSDUH 2015–2016, survey-weighted: past-year any use 12.6% (95% CI 12.2–12.9), 30.6 million adults a year (29.7–31.5 million); only as prescribed 10.4% (10.1–10.7), 25.3 million (24.5–26.1); misuse 2.2% (2.0–2.3), 5.3 million (5.0–5.6); misuse 17.2% of use. Misuse by age, all adults: 18–25 5.2% (4.8–5.6), 26–34 3.3%, 35–49 1.7%, 50–64 1.4%, 65 or older 0.6% (0.4–0.8); as a share of use 51.0%, 28.6%, 13.8%, 9.7% and 4.4%. Among 2,533 reporting misuse (Table 3): without a prescription 73.9%, in greater amounts 16.0%, more often 10.1%, longer 4.9%, other ways 18.7%. Main reason: relax or relieve tension 47.1%, help with sleep 26.6%, get high 11.6%, feelings or emotions 10.1%, experiment 6.0%, effects of another drug 1.6%, hooked 0.6% (sum 103.6%, editors' calculation); ages 18–49 against 50 or older: get high 13.9% against 3.0% (OR 0.19, p = .003; interval printed as .07 to 56), sleep 22.4% against 41.7% (OR 2.48, 1.83–3.35), relax 48.6% against 41.7% (OR 0.76, 0.53–1.08). Source: free from a friend or relative 53.2%, bought from one 12.3%, stolen from one 3.3% (68.8%, editors' sum), one clinician 19.5%, two or more clinicians 0.9%, bought from a dealer or stranger 7.7%, stolen from a health care setting 0.1% (97.0% in all, editors' sum). Medication misused: alprazolam 75.1%, diazepam 20.5%, clonazepam 20.0%, lorazepam 15.4%. DSM-IV past-year abuse 4.6% (3.7–5.6), dependence 6.8% (5.6–8.2); mean days of misuse in the past month 5.4 (SE 0.3). Misuse against use as prescribed, adjusted OR: 65 or older against 18–25 0.23 (0.15–0.34); women 0.74 (0.61–0.90); alcohol abuse or dependence 2.31 (1.73–3.09); marijuana abuse or dependence 2.39 (1.62–3.52); prescription opioid misuse 4.11 (3.26–5.18), abuse or dependence 4.81 (3.45–6.72), use as prescribed 0.69 (0.57–0.84); prescription stimulant misuse 2.46 (1.85–3.27), abuse or dependence 3.40 (1.72–6.70), use as prescribed 0.90 (0.74–1.09).

evidence.locator: Methods, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Methods › Benzodiazepine Use or Misuse, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Cross-sectional analysis of the 2015 and 2016 National Survey on Drug Use and Health (NSDUH): a 50-state multistage area probability sample of the US civilian non-institutionalized population, administered by RTI International for SAMHSA, answered in two computer-assisted parts, one private and audio-assisted to encourage honest reporting of illicit drug use; 86,186 adults. Benzodiazepine use counted when named in the tranquilizer (anxiety or muscle spasm) and sedative (insomnia) items (10,290 people; details in an online supplement). Since the 2015 redesign misuse means any use other than as a doctor directed: without a prescription, in greater amounts, more often or longer than prescribed, or in any other way; anyone reporting any past-year misuse counts as misusing, even if they also used the drug as prescribed. People reporting misuse were asked its manner, their reasons (to relax, to experiment, to get high, for sleep, for emotions, to counter the effect of another drug, because they were hooked, or another reason) and the source; abuse and dependence by DSM-IV criteria.

risk_of_bias.note: JBI prevalence checklist moderate (card sc_maust_2019): a national probability sample, one instrument across both years and design-based weights, with a private computer section for drug questions; but everything is self-report without checks, response rates are not given, and misuse is defined broadly, putting taking extra of one's own prescription, taking a relative's pill to sleep and taking one to get high in one category, which the statement says. Under-reporting and non-response would more likely lower the misuse figure than change the order of reasons or sources. Not downgraded.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: US adults living in households in 2015–2016, and benzodiazepines in general (three in four people who misused one had misused alprazolam), not Xanax alone and not other countries.

imprecision.note: 2,533 people reporting misuse and 86,186 respondents; intervals are narrow for the overall figures. The figures for ages 50 or older rest on 176 people and are given only as a comparison.

publication_bias.note: Not applicable to an analysis of a national survey.

grade.reasoning: Descriptive (prevalence, and self-reported reasons and sources, in a national survey): starts low and is never upgraded; not downgraded (see the domain notes). The reasons are people's own answers to a list and are worded as such; their printed shares add to 103.6%, which the statement says, so they cannot be read as exactly one reason per person, but the order (relaxing, then sleep, then getting high) does not depend on the extra 3.6 points. The associations with other substances are cross-sectional and show nothing about cause. The authors' suggestion that some misuse reflects poor access to care is given as their untested suggestion. The abstract's advice to monitor patients also prescribed opioids or stimulants is left out, because the paper's own Table 2 does not support it (prescribed opioid use went with lower odds of misuse, prescribed stimulant use with no difference). Status single study: one analysis of one survey's first two years after its redesign.
